The Company Appeal (hereinafter referred to as "Appeal") is filed by Mr.
Mohit Prajapati the authorized signatory of the Appellant, under section 61 of
the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("Code/IBC") against the
impugned order dated 13.04.2026 passed by the National Company Law
Tribunal, Mumbai Bench Court-IV in IA/2828/2025 in CP(IB) No. 3138

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 2 of 33

(MB)/2019, denying the Appellant the right to realize its security interest and
refusing to exclude the hypothecated assets from the liquidation estate.
Submissions of the Appellant / Tata Capital Ltd
2.
The Appellant, Tata Capital Limited, had sanctioned various credit
facilities in favour of the Corporate Debtor. Pursuant to the same, several loan
documents were executed between the parties. On account of the said
documents, specific equipment and assets of the Corporate Debtor stood
validly and legally hypothecated in favour of the Appellant, which created a
secured interest in favour of the Appellant. The Corporate Debtor committed
defaults in repayment of the outstanding dues, and its loan accounts were
classified as NPA. Due to this, CIRP and subsequent liquidation proceedings
were initiated against the Corporate Debtor. Corporate Debtor was placed
under liquidation under Section 33(1) of the Code. Mr. Sanjay Ramdas
Mahajan was appointed as Liquidator. Accordingly, the Appellant duly filed
its claim in Form-D as a secured financial creditor and disclosed the details
of the assets and security interest created in its favour. The Appellant had
consistently communicated to the liquidator that it had elected not to
relinquish its security interest and intended to realize the hypothecated assets
independently. The Liquidator failed to verify and hand over the hypothecated
assets to the Appellant and instead sought to include the same in the
liquidation estate and proposed sale process, contrary to the statutory
mandate of Section 52 of the Code. The Appellant submits that its
participation in Stakeholders' Consultation Committee Meetings (SCC)
meetings was without prejudice to its rights and cannot be construed as a
relinquishment of security interest. The Adjudicating Authority, while passing

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 3 of 33

the Impugned Order dated 13.04.2026, failed to appreciate that the Appellant,
being a secured creditor who had not relinquished its security interest, was
legally entitled to realize the secured assets outside the liquidation estate.
Being aggrieved by the said Impugned Order, the Appellant has preferred the
present Appeal seeking setting aside of the Impugned Order to the extent it
denies the Appellant’s right to realize its secured assets and seeking directions
to the Liquidator to exclude the hypothecated assets from the liquidation
estate and hand over the same to the Appellant for enforcement of its security
interest. The Appellant is a secured financial creditor with a valid and
subsisting hypothecation over specific equipment, by virtue of the Terms and
Conditions of the Loan Cum Hypothecation cum Guarantee Agreement dated
11th December, 2018 along with other loan documents. Despite such material
being available, the Adjudicating Authority failed to consider the same in its
proper perspective and instead proceeded to deny the Appellant its statutory
rights. The Appellant claims that in Form – D it had clearly stated that it had
not relinquished its security interest. The Appellant only after rejection of the
scheme, sought to enforce the security interest vide Email dated 19th
February, 2025 which is after 6 months from the liquidation commencement
date. In treating the alleged non-disclosure or incomplete disclosure in the
claim form is not determinative of the Appellant’s rights, without considering
that the existence of the security interest which was otherwise fully
established through contemporaneous loan documents which were duly
exhibited in the Interlocutory Application No. 2828 of 2025, and was never
disputed by the Liquidator or any other stakeholder. Adjudicating Authority

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 4 of 33

failed to properly adjudicate whether a procedural lapse, if any, can override
substantive rights under the Code. The Appellant’s participation in the
Stakeholders’ Consultation Committee is not inconsistent with its intention
to enforce its security interest. The Liquidator with an alleged intention, never
recorded the intention of the Appellants’ participation in SCC meetings itself
speaks volume. The SCC is merely consultative and does not determine or
extinguish the rights of secured creditors. The SCC had not taken any
substantive steps since the settlement and compromise arrangement was
being considered by the SCC in all the meetings. Only in 5th SCC meeting
dated 4th February, 2025 the compromise and arrangement scheme came to
be rejected. As the Scheme of compromise and arrangement came to be
rejected that Appellant once again vide email dated 19th February, 2025
categorically intimated to the liquidator that the Appellant has not
relinquished its rights. An email dated 19th February, 2025 is a valid legal and
enforceable correspondence in order to substantiate the rights of Appellant to
not relinquish their rights over secured assets. Instead of verifying and giving
effect to the Appellant’s security interest, improperly deferred the issue to the
Stakeholders’ Consultation Committee. The Appellant had duly intimated the
Liquidator, through Form D, of its status as a secured creditor and its decision
regarding relinquishment of the secured assets. The core issue requiring
consideration was whether the Liquidator had acted in accordance with his
statutory obligations under the Code and whether his conduct had caused
prejudice to the Appellant’s rights. However, these aspects have not been
adequately considered or addressed in the impugned order. Learned

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 5 of 33

Adjudicating Authority has also erred in attributing undue significance to the
timing of the Appellant’s formal assertion of its rights, without considering
the surrounding circumstances, including the pendency of the compromise
and arrangement proposal under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013.
The fact in issue arises from whether the timing of such assertion can be
construed as a waiver or abandonment of rights, particularly when no
prejudice is shown to have been caused to the liquidation process. There is
absence of any competing claims or third-party rights in respect of the
hypothecated assets at the time when the Appellant sought to enforce its
security interest. In the absence of such competing equities, the Appellant
ought to have been permitted to realize its secured assets independently. The
Ld. Adjudicating Authority has erred in law in holding that the Appellant failed
to assert its security interest on account of alleged deficiencies in Form D,
and in concluding that the entries at Serial Nos. 8 and 8A are complementary
to each other, without appreciating that the Appellant had expressly stated
that it had not relinquished its security interest, thereby clearly evidencing its
intention to realize the same under Section 52 of the Insolvency and
Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The Ld. Adjudicating Authority have erred in finding
that Appellant’s continued participation in SCC meetings, without objection
to its inclusion undermines the contention of the Appellant to stand outside
the liquidation process to enforce the security interest under Section 52 of the
Code. The Hon’ble Adjudicating Authority has erred in finding that the
Appellant was liable to pay the amounts specified in sub regulation 2 of the
Regulation 21A of Liquidation Process Regulations though the Asset was in

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 6 of 33

the custody of Liquidator and the scheme of compromise and arrangement
under section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 was under consideration.

3.
The Learned Adjudicating Authority erred in law in holding that the
Appellant failed to assert its security interest on account of alleged
deficiencies in Form D filed with the liquidator. The Appellant submits that in
Form D, at Serial No. 8A, which specifically requires disclosure as to whether
the security interest has been relinquished, the Appellant has unequivocally
answered "No". This clearly evidences the Appellant’s intention not to
relinquish its security interest over the hypothecated assets and to instead
exercise its rights in terms of Section 52 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy
Code, 2016. The Appellant submits that the Learned Adjudicating Authority
gravely erred in placing undue reliance on the entry at Serial No. 8 of Form
D, which allegedly indicated that no security was held, without appreciating
that such an entry, even if assumed to be incomplete or inadvertent, cannot
override the substantive facts and documentary evidence on record. The
Adjudicating Authority failed to adopt a holistic and harmonious reading of
the Form, particularly when Serial No. 8A unequivocally records that the
Appellant had not relinquished its security interest. However, it is submitted
that Serial Number 8 deals with the "details of the Security held, the value of
the security, and the date it was given" and Serial Number 8A deals with the
details of "whether security interest relinquished". Thus the Ld. Adjudicating
Authority failed to consider that both the information sought in format of
Form D are distinct in nature and can never be complimentary to each other.
In view of the aforesaid, the finding of the Learned Adjudicating Authority that

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 7 of 33

the Appellant failed to assert its security interest in Form D and/ or stipulated
time as per the Code and Regulations is wholly erroneous, contrary to the
material on record, and suffers from non-application of mind. The Impugned
Order proceeds on an overly technical and isolated reading of Form D, while
completely disregarding the express declaration of non-relinquishment as well
as the extensive documentary evidence establishing the Appellant’s secured
status. The Appellant states that such an approach defeats the substantive
rights of the Appellant under Section 52 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy
Code, 2016 and is therefore liable to be set aside, with appropriate directions
recognizing the Appellant’s right to realize its security interest outside the
liquidation estate.

4.
The Ld. Adjudicating Authority erred in law in placing reliance on
Regulation 31A(2) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 to hold
that the Appellant’s participation in the Stakeholders’ Consultation
Committee, including in deliberating the Scheme of Compromise &
Arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013, undermines the
contention of the Appellant to explore to enforce its Security Interest under
Section 52 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The Appellant
submits that the Impugned Order is ex facie erroneous in law inasmuch as it
proceeds on a wrong interpretation of Regulation 31A(2) of the IBBI
(Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016. The Learned Adjudicating Authority,
at paragraph 5.8 of the Impugned Order, has held that "as per the first proviso
to Regulation 31A(2), a secured creditor who has not relinquished its security
interest under Section 52 of the IBC is not eligible to be a member of the SCC"

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 8 of 33

and that the Appellant’s "continued participation in SCC meetings, without
objection to its inclusion, undermines the contention that the Appellant
always sought to stand outside the liquidation process to enforce security
under Section 52 of the Code." This finding is, with respect, wholly erroneous.
The Appellant submits that Section 52 of the Code confers an unequivocal
and independent statutory right upon a secured creditor to either relinquish
its security interest to the liquidation estate or to realize the same outside the
liquidation process. This right is absolute in nature and is not made subject
to participation or non-participation in the SCC. The Hon’ble Supreme Court
in Action Ispat and Power Private Limited v. Shyam Metalics and Energy
Limited [(2021) 2 SCC 641] has, at paragraph 4 of the judgment, expressly
held that "the primary focus of the legislation is to ensure revival and
continuation of the corporate debtor by protecting the corporate debtor from
its own management and from a corporate death by liquidation. The Code is
thus a beneficial legislation which puts the corporate debtor back on its feet,
not being a mere recovery legislation for creditors." This principle, affirmed
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court, has direct bearing on the present case. The
Appellant submits that participation in SCC meetings, including deliberations
pertaining to a scheme of compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of
the Companies Act, 2013, cannot be construed as an election to relinquish
security or as a waiver of rights under Section 52 of the Code. Such
participation is merely a commercial and protective step undertaken to
safeguard the creditor’s interests and remain apprised of developments in the
liquidation process. It is relevant to note that the NCLAT, in Y. Shivram

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 9 of 33

Prasad v. S. Dhanapal & Ors. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 224
of 2018, decided 28.02.2019], has held that during the liquidation process,
before proceeding to sell assets of the Corporate Debtor, the Liquidator is
required to take steps under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 for the
purpose of revival, and that creditors and stakeholders are expected to
participate in this process. The Appellant further submits that the Learned
Adjudicating Authority has failed to adopt a harmonious construction of the
statutory framework. It is well settled that subordinate legislation, including
Regulation 31A, cannot override or curtail substantive rights conferred under
the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code,
2016. The Appellant states that Regulation 31A(2) of the Liquidation Process
Regulations, being subordinate legislation, must be read harmoniously with
and be subservient to Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013, which
mandates consultation and approval of all classes of creditors. Exclusion of
secured creditors from deliberation while requiring their approval may lead to
procedural inconsistencies, inefficiencies, and a risk of failure of the scheme.
Therefore, Regulation 31A must be read in harmony with Section 230 of the
Companies Act, 2013.

5.
The Appellant further relies upon the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme
Court in Swiss Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India [Writ Petition (Civil)
No. 99 of 2018], wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court, while explaining the
very object and scheme of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, has
categorically held that the primary focus of the Code is revival and
continuation of the Corporate Debtor and not its liquidation.

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 10 of 33

“12. It can thus be seen that the primary focus of the legislation is to ensure
revival and continuation of the corporate debtor by protecting the
corporate debtor from its own management and from a corporate death
by liquidation. The Code is thus a beneficial legislation which puts the
corporate debtor back on its feet, not being a mere recovery legislation for
creditors. The interests of the corporate debtor have, therefore, been
bifurcated and separated from that of its promoters / those who are in
management. Thus, the resolution process is not adversarial to the
corporate debtor but, in fact, protective of its interests. The moratorium
imposed by Section 14 is in the interest of the corporate debtor itself,
thereby preserving the assets of the corporate debtor during the
resolution process. The timelines within which the resolution process is to
take place again protects the corporate debtor’s assets from further
dilution, and also protects all its creditors and workers by seeing that the
resolution process goes through as fast as possible so that another
management can, through its entrepreneurial skills, resuscitate the
corporate debtor to achieve all these ends.”

6.
In view of the aforesaid Swiss Ribbons (Supra), the Appellant submits
that participation in the Stakeholders’ Consultation Committee and
deliberations pertaining to the Scheme of Compromise and Arrangement
under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be construed as waiver,
abandonment, or relinquishment of the Appellant’s independent statutory
rights under Section 52 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. On the
contrary, the Appellant’s participation was in furtherance of the very objective
of the Code, namely preservation, revival, and value maximization of the
Corporate Debtor. The Learned Adjudicating Authority therefore erred in
drawing an adverse inference against the Appellant merely on account of its
participation in the SCC proceedings, especially when the Appellant had

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 11 of 33

consistently maintained that it had not relinquished its security interest and
intended to realize the same in accordance with law. The Appellant submits
that the interpretation adopted by the Learned Adjudicating Authority leads
to manifestly absurd consequences. If participation in the SCC were to be
treated as relinquishment or as conduct inconsistent with a Section 52
election, it would effectively compel secured creditors to abstain from all
consultative processes in order to preserve their statutory rights during the
deliberations under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013. No secured
creditor could participate in a Section 230 revival process which is the legal
framework for the revival of the Corporate Debtor and not the death of the
Corporate Debtor. This creates an impossible and legally incoherent position
for secured creditors, which is neither contemplated by the statute nor
supported by any judicial precedent, and is liable to be set aside. In view of
the aforesaid, it is submitted that the finding of the Learned Adjudicating
Authority at paragraphs 5.8 and 5.10 of the Impugned Order that the
Appellant’s participation in the SCC is inconsistent with its right under
Section 52 of the Code is wholly erroneous, perverse, and unsustainable in
law. Accordingly, the Appellant submits that the Impugned Order deserves to
be set aside to this extent, with appropriate directions recognizing that
participation in the Stakeholders’ Consultation Committee including in
deliberations pertaining to a Section 230 Scheme of Compromise and
Arrangement does not amount to relinquishment or waiver of security
interest, and that the Appellant is entitled to realize its security interest

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 12 of 33

independently in accordance with Section 52 of the Insolvency and
Bankruptcy Code, 2016.

7.
The Hon’ble Adjudicating Authority erred in law in denying the
Appellant the right to realize its security interest. The Appellant had, at all
material times, expressly and consistently asserted its intention to stand
outside the liquidation estate and realize its security interest under Section
52 of the Code. Moreover, by participating in the SCC Meetings the Appellant
submits that such intention was communicated during SCC meetings as well
as through a formal email dated 19th February 2025, which unequivocally
invoked its rights over the hypothecated equipment. The Appellant submits
that upon such intimation, the Respondent was statutorily bound under
Section 52(3) of the Code to verify the security interest and permit the
Appellant to realize the same. Instead, the Respondent failed to discharge this
obligation and improperly subjected the Appellant’s statutory rights to the
deliberations of the SCC, which has no jurisdiction in law to decide or approve
such rights. There is no requirement under the Code for SCC approval for
enforcement of security interest by a secured creditor. The Appellant submits
that the impugned findings effectively defeat the statutory scheme of Section
52 and render the Appellant’s independent right illusory. The mere
participation in SCC meetings, of compromise and settlement arrangement
under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 proceedings, cannot be
construed as waiver or relinquishment of security. The finding to the contrary
is inconsistent with the legal framework of the Code that seeks to revive the
Corporate Debtor. Accordingly, the Appellant submits that the impugned

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 13 of 33

findings are based on a misapplication of the statutory framework, disregard
of material evidence, and an incorrect understanding of the role of the SCC,
and are therefore liable to be set aside.

8.
The Appellant submits that on the grounds more particularly
elaborated, and in the facts narrated hereinabove, the Appellant has made
out a good case for the Impugned Order to be set aside.
Submissions of the Respondent / Liquidator
9.
Respondent contends that the appeal is without merit, based on
incorrect facts, unsubstantiated contentions, and a complete misreading of
legal provisions.

10.

11.
The aforesaid chronology clearly demonstrates that the Appellant had,
at all material times, elected to participate in the liquidation process as a
stakeholder and acted consistently with such election.

12.
The Appellant failed to mention its intention to enforce its security in
Form D under Regulation 21A of IBBI Liquidation Process Regulations, 2016.
There is material omission in Form D. The Form D at Sr. No.8, as submitted
by the Appellant had intimated ‘NIL’ in response to the details of the security
held by it. Thereafter, in Sr. No. 8A, the Appellant had indicated ‘No’ in
response to whether it relinquished its interest. The Ld. Adjudicating
Authority rightly observed that Sr. No 8 and 8A are complementary to each
other and are to be read together. When so done, the clear impression is that
the Appellant has not indicated any security that its willing to relinquish. In

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 15 of 33

terms of Regulation 21 of the Liquidation Regulations, the Appellant was
required to inform the Liquidator of its decision, which it has failed to do so.
The Appellant’s assertion that Form D duly communicated its decision is
contrary to the express entries therein.

13.
The Appellant’s omission was neither merely procedural nor
inconsequential. Regulation 21A expressly requires the secured creditor to
communicate its decision in Form C or Form D within the stipulated period
and prescribes the consequence of non-intimation. Documents evidencing the
creation of security cannot substitute for the required election as to whether
such security would be relinquished or realised. Ld. Adjudicating Authority
therefore committed no error in distinguishing between the existence of
security and the exercise of the option under Section 52.

14.
The Appellant actively participated in the SCC Meetings without
attempting to correct this position. The Appellant continued participating in
SCC meetings and exercised voting rights. The Ld. Adjudicating Authority also
correctly observed that a secured creditor not relinquishing its interest is not
entitled to participate in SCC under Regulation 31A(2).

15.
Ld. Adjudicating Authority did not hold that participation in the SCC,
by itself, extinguished the Appellant’s security interest. The Appellant’s
participation and exercise of voting rights were correctly considered as
material conduct inconsistent with its subsequent claim that it had always
elected to stand outside the liquidation estate, particularly in view of the first
proviso to Regulation 31A(2). The allegation that the Respondent intentionally

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 16 of 33

failed to record the Appellant’s purported position is denied as false and
unsupported.

16.
Respondent also contends that there was delay in exercising option.
The Appellant only chose to exercise its right on 19.02.2025 after rejection of
the Compromise Scheme on 04.02.2025. The same is after 6 months from
liquidation commencement date. In these circumstances, the Ld. Adjudicating
Authority rightly held that Regulation 21A (2) was never complied with by the
Appellant.

17.
The Appellant did not expressly or consistently assert an intention to
stand outside the liquidation estate. No such assertion is borne out from Form
D or the contemporaneous minutes of the SCC meetings. The email dated
19.02.2025 was the first clear written demand for exclusion and delivery of
the assets and was issued after expiry of the statutory period.

18.
Regarding alleged oral intimations of the Appellant in relation to its
intention to enforce it security interest, the said contention is a bald and
unsupported assertion and finds no mention in the contemporaneous
minutes of the SCC meetings. The Appellant admittedly communicated its
alleged election in writing for the first time only by its email dated 19.02.2025,
after rejection of the Scheme of Compromise on 04.02.2025 and more than
six months after the liquidation commencement date. The allegation that the
Respondent deliberately failed to record any purported oral intimation is false,
baseless and denied.

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 17 of 33

19.
The email dated 19.02.2025 constituted a belated attempt by the
Appellant to alter the position adopted by it throughout the liquidation
process and could not cure its failure to intimate its decision in the manner
and within the period prescribed under Regulation 21A. The obligation of the
Respondent to verify a security interest under Section 52(3) arises where a
secured creditor has validly and timely elected to realize such security interest
in accordance with the Code and the Liquidation Regulations. The Appellant
having failed to make such an election cannot invoke Section 52(3) in
isolation.

20.
The email dated 19.02.2025 was not a reiteration of any earlier valid
election but was the first written communication whereby the Appellant
sought exclusion and delivery of the assets. The timing of the email, shortly
after rejection of the Scheme, supports the finding that the Appellant sought
to alter its position only after the possibility of revival through the Scheme
had failed. Ld. Adjudicating Authority duly considered the email dated
19.02.2025 but correctly held that it was issued beyond the prescribed period
and could not retrospectively cure the Appellant’s non-compliance. The
Appellant’s substantive rights were required to be exercised subject to the
procedural and temporal framework prescribed by the Code and the
Liquidation Regulations.

21.
It is further denied that the Respondent subjected the Appellant’s
alleged right to the approval of the SCC. The issue was placed before the SCC
only in the context of its effect upon the liquidation estate and the ongoing

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 18 of 33

liquidation process, and not for adjudication of the Appellant’s rights. The
matter was discussed in the SCC because exclusion of the assets would
materially affect the liquidation estate and the interests of all stakeholders.
No approval of the SCC was treated as a statutory precondition for exercise of
rights under Section 52.

22.
The Appellant’s highly belated assertion, made only after the rejection
of the Scheme of Compromise, is plainly an afterthought and cannot be
permitted to unsettle the liquidation process or defeat the consequences of its
own omissions and conduct. The findings returned by the Ld. Adjudicating
Authority are therefore fully borne out from the record and warrant no
interference by this Hon’ble Tribunal.

23.
While the Appellant’s status as a secured financial creditor was not in
dispute, the mere existence of a security interest does not dispense with the
mandatory requirement of making and communicating an election under
Regulation 21A. It is specifically denied that the Appellant informed the
Respondent of its decision within time or that the Respondent deliberately
delayed, obstructed or prevented the Appellant from realizing its security
interest. The Respondent has acted bona fide and strictly in furtherance of
his statutory duties as Liquidator and in the interests of the liquidation
process and all stakeholders.

24.
Granting the relief sought at this belated stage would not only reward
the Appellant’s own omissions but would also unsettle the steps already
undertaken by the Liquidator. It would grossly delay the liquidation process

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 19 of 33

and prejudice the rights and interests of the other stakeholders who have
proceeded on the basis of the Appellant’s conduct and the existing
composition of the liquidation estate. The Appeal is therefore liable to be
dismissed with exemplary costs.

25.
The assets were legitimately treated as forming part of the liquidation
estate consequent upon the Appellant’s failure to intimate its election within
the prescribed period and its subsequent conduct throughout the liquidation
process. The Appellant is therefore not entitled to seek exclusion or delivery
of the assets at this belated stage. The Ld. Adjudicating Authority has rightly
declined to exercise jurisdiction in favour of the Appellant.

26.
Ld. Adjudicating Authority rightly held that Regulation 21A (2) was
never complied with by the Appellant. Despite having full knowledge of the
liquidation proceedings, the taking over and valuation of the assets, and the
constitution and functioning of the SCC, the Appellant neither disclosed its
security interest in the prescribed manner nor exercised its alleged right to
realise the same within the stipulated period. It is quite apparent that the
Appellant sought to simultaneously enjoy the benefits of participation in the
liquidation process and preserve an option to withdraw its security at a later
stage depending upon the outcome of the Scheme.

27.
No irreparable harm or prejudice can be alleged by the Appellant on
account of the consequences flowing from its own omissions and conduct. On
the contrary, exclusion of the assets at this advanced stage would severely
prejudice the liquidation process and the interests of the remaining

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 20 of 33

stakeholders, particularly when the liquidation estate, its valuation and the
steps undertaken by the Respondent have proceeded on the basis that the
assets form part thereof. The balance of convenience is entirely against grant
of any relief to the Appellant.

28.
Learned Adjudicating Authority expressly recognized that the Appellant
was a secured financial creditor and thereafter correctly identified the real
issue as being whether the Appellant could, at the belated stage in question,
assert its right to realize the security interest under Section 52. The existence
of the underlying loan and security documents did not, by itself, establish
compliance with the independent statutory requirement of making and
communicating an election under Regulation 21A. The Appellant is
deliberately conflating the existence of a security interest with the timely
exercise of the option to realize such security interest.

29.
The entries made by the Appellant in Form D were contradictory and
failed to disclose the particulars and value of the alleged security interest or
clearly communicate an election to realize the same. The Appellant’s
subsequent participation in the SCC, exercise of voting rights, knowledge of
the Respondent taking custody of the assets and failure to object thereto are
wholly inconsistent with the case now sought to be advanced. There is no
question of any unjust enrichment of the other stakeholders.

30.
The Impugned Order is a reasoned order passed after due consideration
of the pleadings, documents, applicable statutory provisions and conduct of
the parties. Learned Adjudicating Authority has correctly held that the

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 21 of 33

Appellant failed to duly exercise its option under Section 52 read with
Regulation 21A and that its belated attempt to do so could not be accepted.
The allegations of patent illegality, non-application of mind and failure to
consider material documents are false and misconceived.

31.
The Respondent acted in accordance with his statutory duties and
treated the assets as part of the liquidation estate on account of the
Appellant’s failure to validly and timely exercise its option.

32.
The timing of the Appellant’s assertion was not assigned “undue”
significance but was correctly considered in light of the express thirty-day
period prescribed under Regulation 21A (unamended) and the Appellant’s
conduct during the intervening period. Pendency of a Scheme under Section
230 did not place the Liquidation Regulations in abeyance. It is further denied
that no prejudice would be caused to the liquidation process. Exclusion of
substantial assets after custody, valuation and other steps had already been
undertaken would materially disrupt and delay the liquidation and prejudice
the other stakeholders.

33.
Recognition of the Appellant as a secured financial creditor did not
create any legitimate expectation that it could exercise the option under
Section 52 at any time of its choosing. The right under Section 52 is regulated
by Regulation 21A and is subject to compliance with the conditions and
timelines stipulated therein. No enforceable right can arise contrary to the
statutory framework.

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 22 of 33

34.
The existence or absence of competing security interests is irrelevant to
the Appellant’s failure to validly exercise its option under Section 52 read with
Regulation 21A.

35.
Regulation 31A(2) neither overrides nor curtails Section 230 of the
Companies Act, 2013. It merely regulates the constitution and membership
of the SCC during liquidation. Consultation or approval required under a
Scheme of Compromise is governed by the applicable provisions of the
Companies Act and does not confer an independent right upon an otherwise
ineligible secured creditor to remain a member of the SCC. The alleged
inconsistency is artificial and misconceived.

36.
The reliance placed upon Action Ispat and Power Private Limited
(supra) is misconceived and does not support the proposition that a secured
creditor may disregard the mandatory requirements governing exercise of its
option.

37.
The decision in Y. Shivram Prasad (supra) concerning exploration of
revival through Section 230 does not dispense with compliance by secured
creditors with Regulation 21A or permit an otherwise ineligible secured
creditor to participate and vote in the SCC while simultaneously claiming to
stand outside the liquidation estate.

38.
The reliance upon Swiss Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. (supra) is misplaced. The
general object of revival and value maximisation cannot be invoked to defeat
specific provisions governing liquidation or the timelines and consequences

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 23 of 33

prescribed under Regulation 21A. In fact, permitting the Appellant to
withdraw substantial assets from the liquidation estate after expiry of the
prescribed period would undermine certainty, value maximisation and timely
completion of the liquidation process.

39.
It is submitted that there are no absurd results from application of
Regulation 31A(2). A secured creditor is required to make a clear statutory
election. The consequences of such election, including its eligibility to
participate in the SCC, are expressly provided by law. The alleged difficulty
arises only because the Appellant seeks to simultaneously enjoy the benefits
of participation in the liquidation process and preserve an option to withdraw
its security at a later stage depending upon the outcome of the Scheme.

40.
The Appellant is not entitled to any declaration that its participation in
the SCC was without consequence or to any direction permitting realisation
of the assets outside the liquidation estate. The said declaration, in any event
being contrary to law, is untenable.

41.
The obligation under Section 52(3) cannot be invoked without a valid
election under Section 52 read with Regulation 21A. The Respondent was not
required to permit realisation of security on the basis of an untimely and
legally ineffective communication. It is denied that the Appellant’s rights were
made subject to approval of the SCC.

42.
Ld. Adjudicating Authority did not impose any requirement of SCC
approval. The Appellant’s application was dismissed because it had failed to

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 24 of 33

validly and timely exercise its option, had participated throughout the
liquidation process and had failed to comply with Regulation 21A(2).

43.
The Appellant cannot rely upon the proposed Scheme under Section
230 to explain away its non-compliance or to retrospectively convert its
participation in the SCC into an act undertaken without prejudice to a
purported earlier election which was never communicated in terms of the
statute.

44.
The Appellant is not entitled to setting aside of the Impugned Order or
to possession of the alleged hypothecated equipment. Grant of such relief
would permit the Appellant to circumvent the mandatory requirements and
consequences prescribed under Regulation 21A, unsettle the liquidation
estate after substantial steps have already been undertaken, delay completion
of the liquidation process and seriously prejudice the rights of the other
stakeholders.

45.
It is most respectfully submitted that the Appeal is liable to be
dismissed with exemplary costs.
Analysis and Findings
46.
Appellant/Tata Capital Ltd. claims that it is a secured financial creditor
having a valid hypothecation over the assets of the Corporate Debtor. It
submits that it had filed its claim in Form D and had stated that it had not
relinquished its security interest. According to the Appellant, its participation
in the stakeholders' Consultation Committee (SCC) meetings and in the
consideration of the Scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 25 of 33

was without prejudice to its right under Section 52 of the Code. It submits
that the email dated 19.02.2025 was a valid intimation of its decision to
realize the secured assets outside the liquidation estate after the Scheme was
rejected. The Appellant further contends that the existence of the security
interest is established by the loan and hypothecation documents and that any
deficiency in Form D cannot defeat its substantive right under Section 52. It
also relies upon Action Ispat and Power Private Limited (supra), Y.
Shivram Prasad (supra) and Swiss Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. (supra) to submit that
the Code is intended to promote revival and value maximization and that
participation in the revival process cannot amount to waiver or
relinquishment of its security interest.

47.
The Respondent/Liquidator claims that the Appellant did not validly
and timely exercise the option contemplated by Section 52 of the Code read
with Regulation 21A of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016. The
liquidation commenced on 13.08.2024, whereas the Appellant submitted
Form D on 01.10.2024 and did not communicate within the prescribed period
its decision to realize the security outside the liquidation estate. In Form D,
Serial No. 8 was stated as 'NIL', while Serial No. 8A stated 'No' to
relinquishment, which, according to the Respondent, did not constitute a
clear election to stand outside the liquidation estate. The Appellant thereafter
participated in the SCC meetings and exercised its voting rights, including in
relation to the Scheme of Compromise under Section 230 of the Companies
Act, 2013. The Respondent submits that the first clear written request for
exclusion and delivery of the assets was made only by email dated

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 26 of 33

19.02.2025, after the Scheme had failed on 04.02.2025 and more than six
months after commencement of liquidation. The Respondent therefore
contends that the belated email could not cure the statutory non-compliance.
It is further submitted that the existence of a security interest is distinct from
the timely exercise of the statutory option and that Section 52(3) cannot be
invoked without a valid election under Regulation 21A. The Respondent
submits that the Impugned Order is reasoned and calls for no interference.

48.
We have considered the submissions of the learned Counsel for the
Appellant and the learned Liquidator and have perused the record placed
before us. The principal question which arises for consideration is whether
the Appellant, as a secured creditor, validly and within the prescribed period
exercised its option under Section 52 of the Code to stand outside the
liquidation estate and realize the secured assets.

49.
There is no dispute that the Appellant is a secured financial creditor
and that the hypothecation documents relied upon by it record a security
interest over the concerned assets. However, the existence of a security
interest and the exercise of the statutory option to realize that security outside
the liquidation estate are two distinct matters. The present Appeal is required
to be examined with reference to the latter issue.

50.
Before proceeding further let us extract the provisions of Section 52(2)
of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and also Regulation 21A, 31A(2) and
39BA of Liquidation Process Regulations, which provides for the presumption
of security interest and which are helpful in deciding the case in hand.

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 27 of 33

“52.
Secured creditor in the liquidation proceedings
(1)
A secured creditor in the liquidation proceedings may—
(a)
relinquish its security interest to the liquidation estate and
receive proceeds from the sale of assets by the liquidator in
the manner specified in section 53; or
(b)
realise its security interest in the manner specified in this
section.
(2)
Where the secured creditor realizes security interest under clause
(b) of sub-section (1), he shall inform the liquidator of such security interest
and identify the asset subject to such security interest to be realized.”
[Prior to amendment of 2026]
21A.
21A. Presumption of security interest.
(1)
A secured creditor shall inform the liquidator of its decision to
relinquish its security interest to the liquidation estate or realise
its security interest, as the case may be, in Form C or Form D of
Schedule II.

Provided that, where a secured creditor does not intimate its decision
within thirty days from the liquidation commencement date, the assets
covered under the security interest shall be deemed to be relinquished to
the liquidation estate.”
[Prior to latest amendments of 2026]
Regulation 31A: Stakeholders’ consultation committee.
(1) XXX
(2) The voting share of a member of the consultation committee shall be
in proportion to his admitted claim in the total admitted claim:
Provided a secured creditor who has not relinquished his security interest
under section 52 shall not be part of the consultation committee;

Provided that the promoters, directors, partners or their representatives
may attend the meeting of the consultation committee, but shall not have
any right to vote.

Provided further that a financial creditor or his representative, if he is a
related party of the corporate debtor, shall not have right to vote.
(3)....”

“Regulation 39BA: Assessment of Compromise or Arrangement.
39BA. (1) While deciding to liquidate the corporate debtor under section
33, the committee shall examine whether to explore compromise or

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 28 of 33

arrangement as referred to under sub -regulation (1) of regulation 2B of
the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Liquidation Process)
Regulation, 2016 and the resolution professional shall submit the
committee’s recommendation to the Adjudicating Authority while filing
application under section 33.
(2) Where a recommendation has been made under sub-regulation (1), the
resolution professional and the committee shall keep exploring the
possibility of compromise or arrangement during the period the
application to liquidate the corporate debtor is pending before the
Adjudicating Authority.”

51.
The liquidation commenced on 13.08.2024. The record shows that the
Appellant submitted Form D on 01.10.2024. In the said Form, Serial No. 8
contained an entry of 'NIL' in relation to the details of security held, whereas
Serial No. 8A contained the answer 'No' to the question whether the security
interest had been relinquished. The Adjudicating Authority considered these
entries together and held that the Appellant had not clearly communicated
the option to realize its security interest outside the liquidation estate. We find
no error in this approach.

52.
The statutory scheme requires a secured creditor who seeks to stand
outside the liquidation estate to exercise and communicate its option within
the prescribed period. The Appellant admittedly did not make a clear written
request for exclusion of the hypothecated assets and their delivery for
realization within that period. The first clear written communication relied
upon by the Appellant is the email dated 19.02.2025. This communication
was issued after the Scheme of Compromise under Section 230 of the
Companies Act, 2013 had been rejected on 04.02.2025. Thus, the Appellant

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 29 of 33

did not opt to stand outside the liquidation estate within the prescribed thirty
days and waited until the Scheme had failed.

53.
The explanation of the Appellant that it had orally communicated its
intention or that the entries in Form D were sufficient cannot be accepted in
the facts of the present case. There is no contemporaneous record placed
before us showing a clear and valid election within the prescribed period. The
subsequent email dated 19.02.2025 cannot retrospectively cure the failure to
exercise the statutory option within time.

54.
The participation of the Appellant in the SCC meetings is also a relevant
circumstance. The Appellant remained a member of the SCC, attended its
meetings and exercised its voting rights – to further confirm that it has
relinquished its security interest else would not have been part of SCC per
Regulation 31A. The Appellant was aware of the taking of custody of the assets
and the valuation process. It did not, during the relevant period, take the
position in a manner and within the time prescribed by Regulation 21A that
the assets were to be excluded from the liquidation estate for independent
realization. The conduct of the Appellant, therefore, has to be considered
along with the entries made in Form D and the belated email dated
19.02.2025.

55.
We are unable to accept the submission that the pendency of the
Scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 kept the statutory
requirements of the liquidation process in abeyance. The consideration of a
Scheme for revival and value maximization does not dispense with the

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 30 of 33

statutory requirement applicable to a secured creditor seeking to realize its
security outside the liquidation estate. The Appellant could not retain an
uncommunicated option and seek to exercise it after the Scheme had failed.

56.
The judgments relied upon by the Appellant, including Action Ispat and
Power Private Limited (supra), Y. Shivram Prasad (supra) and Swiss
Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. (supra), emphasize the object of revival, continuation and
value maximization under the Code. Those principles cannot be read as
dispensing with the specific statutory requirements governing the exercise of
an option under Section 52 read with Regulation 21A. The object of the Code
has to operate within the statutory framework governing liquidation.

57.
The submission that no prejudice was caused because there were no
competing claims over the assets also does not advance the Appellant's case.
The requirement of making the election within the prescribed period is part of
the statutory scheme. Its applicability does not depend upon the existence of
a competing security interest. Once the Appellant failed to exercise the option
in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed period, it cannot seek to
revive that option at a later stage on the ground that no third-party equity
had intervened.

58.
We also do not find merit in the contention that the Liquidator made
the Appellant's right subject to approval of the SCC. The record, as noticed in
the submissions of the Liquidator, shows that the issue was considered in the
context of its effect upon the liquidation estate and the interests of the
stakeholders. The Appellant's application was rejected by the Adjudicating

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 31 of 33

Authority primarily because the statutory option had not been validly and
timely exercised. The requirement of SCC approval was not treated as a
statutory precondition for exercise of the right under Section 52.

59.
We further observe that per combined reading of Section 52(2) of the
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and also Regulations 21A, 31A(2) and 39BA
of Liquidation Process Regulations, the Appellant cannot be permitted to
simultaneously participate in the liquidation process and preserve an option
to withdraw the secured assets at a later stage depending upon the result of
the Scheme. Here we observe that the appellant had not relinquished its
security interest and continued to participate in the stakeholder consultation
committee meeting and also participated in the scheme of compromise and
arrangement scheme. Thereafter only, it elected to stand outside, which is
totally impermissible as per the existing Code and regulations. The regulation
governing the scheme of compromise and arrangement (39BA) doesn’t grant
extension of time for Appellant with the security interest to stand out of the
liquidation estate at a later point in time. Such a course would unsettle the
liquidation estate after custody and valuation of the assets and after other
steps in the liquidation process had been undertaken. The Liquidator was
justified in treating the assets as part of the liquidation estate in view of the
Appellant's failure to make a timely and valid election.

60.
The distinction between the existence of a security interest and the
exercise of the statutory option is material. The loan documents may establish
the existence of the security, but they do not by themselves establish

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 32 of 33

compliance with the separate requirement of communicating the election
contemplated by Regulation 21A. The Adjudicating Authority has correctly
applied this distinction.

61.
On an overall consideration of the record, we are satisfied that the
Appellant did not validly exercise its option to stand outside the liquidation
estate within the prescribed thirty days. The Appellant waited until after the
Scheme of Compromise had failed and thereafter sought to assert its right by
email dated 19.02.2025. Such a belated assertion cannot be accepted to the
prejudice of the liquidation process and other stakeholders.

62.
We, therefore, find no infirmity in the Impugned Order dated
13.04.2026 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in IA/2828/2025 in CP(IB)
No. 3138 (MB)/2019. The submissions of the Appellant seeking exclusion of
the hypothecated assets and permission to realize the security interest
outside the liquidation estate are unsustainable. The submissions of the
Liquidator that the Appellant failed to comply with the statutory requirement
and that the belated exercise of the option cannot be permitted are supported
by the statutory scheme and the facts borne out from the record.

63.
In view of the foregoing discussion, we are of the considered view that
the Appeal does not merit interference by this Appellate Tribunal. The
Impugned Order calls for no interference.
Conclusion
64.
For the reasons stated above, the Appeal is dismissed. The Impugned
Order dated 13.04.2026 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026 33 of 33

IA/2828/2025 in CP(IB) No. 3138 (MB)/2019 is affirmed. The Appellant is not
entitled to exclusion of the hypothecated assets from the liquidation estate or
to realize the said assets outside the liquidation process on the basis of its
belated communication dated 19.02.2025.
Order
65.
The Appeal is dismissed. The Impugned Order dated 13.04.2026 passed
by the National Company Law Tribunal in IA/2828/2025 in CP(IB) No. 3138
(MB)/2019 is affirmed. All related IAs are also accordingly disposed of. No
order as to costs.

51.
The liquidation commenced on 13.08.2024. The record shows that the
Appellant submitted Form D on 01.10.2024. In the said Form, Serial No. 8
contained an entry of 'NIL' in relation to the details of security held, whereas
Serial No. 8A contained the answer 'No' to the question whether the security
interest had been relinquished. The Adjudicating Authority considered these
entries together and held that the Appellant had not clearly communicated
the option to realize its security interest outside the liquidation estate. We find
no error in this approach.

52.
The statutory scheme requires a secured creditor who seeks to stand
outside the liquidation estate to exercise and communicate its option within
the prescribed period. The Appellant admittedly did not make a clear written
request for exclusion of the hypothecated assets and their delivery for
realization within that period. The first clear written communication relied
upon by the Appellant is the email dated 19.02.2025. This communication
was issued after the Scheme of Compromise under Section 230 of the
Companies Act, 2013 had been rejected on 04.02.2025. Thus, the Appellant

[PAGE 29]

did not opt to stand outside the liquidation estate within the prescribed thirty
days and waited until the Scheme had failed.

53.
The explanation of the Appellant that it had orally communicated its
intention or that the entries in Form D were sufficient cannot be accepted in
the facts of the present case. There is no contemporaneous record placed
before us showing a clear and valid election within the prescribed period. The
subsequent email dated 19.02.2025 cannot retrospectively cure the failure to
exercise the statutory option within time.

54.
The participation of the Appellant in the SCC meetings is also a relevant
circumstance. The Appellant remained a member of the SCC, attended its
meetings and exercised its voting rights – to further confirm that it has
relinquished its security interest else would not have been part of SCC per
Regulation 31A. The Appellant was aware of the taking of custody of the assets
and the valuation process. It did not, during the relevant period, take the
position in a manner and within the time prescribed by Regulation 21A that
the assets were to be excluded from the liquidation estate for independent
realization. The conduct of the Appellant, therefore, has to be considered
along with the entries made in Form D and the belated email dated
19.02.2025.

55.
We are unable to accept the submission that the pendency of the
Scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 kept the statutory
requirements of the liquidation process in abeyance. The consideration of a
Scheme for revival and value maximization does not dispense with the

[PAGE 30]

statutory requirement applicable to a secured creditor seeking to realize its
security outside the liquidation estate. The Appellant could not retain an
uncommunicated option and seek to exercise it after the Scheme had failed.

56.
The judgments relied upon by the Appellant, including Action Ispat and
Power Private Limited (supra), Y. Shivram Prasad (supra) and Swiss
Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. (supra), emphasize the object of revival, continuation and
value maximization under the Code. Those principles cannot be read as
dispensing with the specific statutory requirements governing the exercise of
an option under Section 52 read with Regulation 21A. The object of the Code
has to operate within the statutory framework governing liquidation.

57.
The submission that no prejudice was caused because there were no
competing claims over the assets also does not advance the Appellant's case.
The requirement of making the election within the prescribed period is part of
the statutory scheme. Its applicability does not depend upon the existence of
a competing security interest. Once the Appellant failed to exercise the option
in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed period, it cannot seek to
revive that option at a later stage on the ground that no third-party equity
had intervened.

58.
We also do not find merit in the contention that the Liquidator made
the Appellant's right subject to approval of the SCC. The record, as noticed in
the submissions of the Liquidator, shows that the issue was considered in the
context of its effect upon the liquidation estate and the interests of the
stakeholders. The Appellant's application was rejected by the Adjudicating

[PAGE 31]

Authority primarily because the statutory option had not been validly and
timely exercised. The requirement of SCC approval was not treated as a
statutory precondition for exercise of the right under Section 52.

59.
We further observe that per combined reading of Section 52(2) of the
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and also Regulations 21A, 31A(2) and 39BA
of Liquidation Process Regulations, the Appellant cannot be permitted to
simultaneously participate in the liquidation process and preserve an option
to withdraw the secured assets at a later stage depending upon the result of
the Scheme. Here we observe that the appellant had not relinquished its
security interest and continued to participate in the stakeholder consultation
committee meeting and also participated in the scheme of compromise and
arrangement scheme. Thereafter only, it elected to stand outside, which is
totally impermissible as per the existing Code and regulations. The regulation
governing the scheme of compromise and arrangement (39BA) doesn’t grant
extension of time for Appellant with the security interest to stand out of the
liquidation estate at a later point in time. Such a course would unsettle the
liquidation estate after custody and valuation of the assets and after other
steps in the liquidation process had been undertaken. The Liquidator was
justified in treating the assets as part of the liquidation estate in view of the
Appellant's failure to make a timely and valid election.

60.
The distinction between the existence of a security interest and the
exercise of the statutory option is material. The loan documents may establish
the existence of the security, but they do not by themselves establish

compliance with the separate requirement of communicating the election
contemplated by Regulation 21A. The Adjudicating Authority has correctly
applied this distinction.

61.
On an overall consideration of the record, we are satisfied that the
Appellant did not validly exercise its option to stand outside the liquidation
estate within the prescribed thirty days. The Appellant waited until after the
Scheme of Compromise had failed and thereafter sought to assert its right by
email dated 19.02.2025. Such a belated assertion cannot be accepted to the
prejudice of the liquidation process and other stakeholders.

62.
We, therefore, find no infirmity in the Impugned Order dated
13.04.2026 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in IA/2828/2025 in CP(IB)
No. 3138 (MB)/2019. The submissions of the Appellant seeking exclusion of
the hypothecated assets and permission to realize the security interest
outside the liquidation estate are unsustainable. The submissions of the
Liquidator that the Appellant failed to comply with the statutory requirement
and that the belated exercise of the option cannot be permitted are supported
by the statutory scheme and the facts borne out from the record.

63.
In view of the foregoing discussion, we are of the considered view that
the Appeal does not merit interference by this Appellate Tribunal. The
Impugned Order calls for no interference.
